title: Learn by Doing: Types, Operators, Input and Output
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then the past question that uses JOptionPane, and the method taught from nothing with every listing run.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, from the two solved papers.

Integer division and the JOptionPane pattern are the two things in this topic that cost whole questions rather than single marks.

lockin.big: "int divided by int is an int. 7 / 2 is 3, and no amount of storing it in a double fixes it after the fact."
lockin.sub: Cast one side first, or use a double literal. JOptionPane reads a String, so parse it with Integer.parseInt or Double.parseDouble.

methodFrames.teach:
The eight primitives are byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean. Whole numbers are int, decimals are double, and everything else is a special case.

public class Divide {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int a = 7, b = 2;        System.out.println(a / b);        double wrong = a / b;        System.out.println(wrong);        double right = (double) a / b;        System.out.println(right);    }}
Output3
3.0
3.5
methodFrames.ask: What do you think this prints, before you look?

methodFrames.teach:
int divided by int is an int, and the fraction is thrown away at the moment of division. Storing the answer in a double afterwards is too late, which is why the second line still prints 3.0.

The fix is to cast BEFORE dividing, or to make one side a double literal: (double) a / b, or a / 2.0.
methodFrames.ask: Now the other arithmetic trap. What does the modulus operator give you, and what is it used for in every exam question about digits?

methodFrames.check: The remainder. n % 10 is the last digit and n / 10 drops it.
methodFrames.teach:
% gives the remainder, and the pair n % 10 and n / 10 is how you take a number apart digit by digit: the first gives the last digit, the second removes it.

public class Digits {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 407, sum = 0;        while (n > 0) {            int digit = n % 10;            sum += digit * digit * digit;            n = n / 10;        }        System.out.println(sum);    }}
Output407
methodFrames.ask: Armstrong numbers, perfect numbers, palindromes and digit counts are all built on that pair. What does this print?

methodFrames.teach:
It prints 407, because 4 cubed plus 0 cubed plus 7 cubed is 407: that is an Armstrong number, and it is a past question in Topic Three.

Now the increment trap. i++ uses the value THEN adds one; ++i adds one THEN uses it.

public class Increment {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int i = 5;        System.out.println(i++);        System.out.println(i);        System.out.println(++i);    }}
Output5
6
7

5, then 6, then 7. Read it as: post increment hands over the old value, pre increment hands over the new one.

One more operator trap: + joins when either side is a String. "total: " + 1 + 2 gives "total: 12", because it works left to right. Bracket the arithmetic.
methodFrames.ask: Now input. This paper's Section C says JOptionPane only. What does showInputDialog return?

methodFrames.teach:
A String, always, exactly like Scanner's nextLine. So it must be parsed: Integer.parseInt(text) or Double.parseDouble(text). Forgetting that is the single most common lost mark in Section C.

The pattern to memorise, since it is not compiled here only because it opens a window:

import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Fees {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String text = JOptionPane.showInputDialog("How many hours?");        int hours = Integer.parseInt(text);        double fee = hours * 150.0;        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Fee: " + fee);        System.exit(0);    }}
methodFrames.ask: Two more lines in that skeleton earn marks. Which, and why?

methodFrames.teach:
import javax.swing.JOptionPane; at the top, and System.exit(0); at the end, which closes the program after the last dialog. Both are on the mark scheme, and both are one line each.

For printed output, printf formats: %d whole number, %.2f two decimals, %s string, %n newline.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Five, 12 marks

scenario.text:
(12 marks)A. A conference organiser needs a program (using JOptionPane only, for all input/output) that prices tickets for a 3-day conference and produces a sales summary. Implement the following four methods.

i.    Create a method that takes in a day number. Use a switch statement to return a base ticket price for Day 1, Day 2, or Day 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly). If the day number is not 1, 2, or 3, throw an IllegalArgumentException.

ii.   Create a method that takes in a tier and a number of days attending. Use nested if-else statements (not a switch, and not independent/separate if checks) to return a discount percentage:

•  Gold, attending all 3 days -> 25%

•  Gold, attending 1-2 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending all 3 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending 1-2 days -> 5%

•  Bronze (any days) -> 0%

•  Any tier string that is not "Gold" or "Silver" must be treated as "Bronze"

The nesting must reflect that "days attending" is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a base price total and a discount percentage and applies the discount to the base price total. If the discounted amount is below 50.0, the method should return 50.0 instead (a price floor).

iv.  main()

•  Ask the user for the number of attendees N (a positive integer).

•  Loop exactly N times. In each iteration, ask for that attendee's number of days attending (an integer from 1 to 3, inclusive) and tier. For each day from 1 up to that attendee's days attending, call the method from part (i) and add the result to that attendee's running base price total (a running total that starts at 0 for each new attendee). Then call the method from part (ii) to get the discount percentage, and the method from part (iii) to get that attendee's final price.

•  Accumulate: (a) total revenue across all attendees, and (b) a running count of how many attendees were Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

v.   After the loop, show one summary dialog with total revenue and the three tier counts.

questions.asked: Shape: Write a program. A full program, marked on structure as much as on logic. The two papers set this shape 17 times between them, 1 of them on this topic.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
GivenA complete pricing specification and the structure of the four methods.
Asked forFour methods plus a main, with the control structure of each dictated: switch in part i, nested if-else in part ii.
The marks12 marks. The structural constraints are marked, so a correct answer written the wrong way loses marks.
WatchPart ii spells out the nesting it wants and then repeats it in a separate sentence, which is the examiner telling you where the marks are. Tier is the outer test, days the inner. Anything not "Gold" or "Silver" falls to Bronze, so that is the else branch, not a third named case.
Taught inUnits 4.2, 4.3, 5.4, 9.4 and F.11.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 12 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q5 a · conference ticket pricing · 12 MARKS
  1. takes a day number, uses a switch to return a base price for Day 1, 2 or 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly); any other day throws IllegalArgumentException;
  2. takes a tier and days attending, and uses nested if-else to return a discount: Gold 3 days 25%, Gold 1-2 days 15%, Silver 3 days 15%, Silver 1-2 days 5%, Bronze 0%, and any tier that is not "Gold" or "Silver" is Bronze. The nesting must reflect that days are only checked within each tier branch;
  3. takes a base total and a discount percentage, applies it, and returns 50.0 if the result would fall below 50.0 (a price floor);
  4. main(): ask for N attendees; loop N times asking days and tier; sum the day prices into a per-attendee base total; get the discount; get the final price; accumulate total revenue and a count of Gold, Silver and Bronze; then show one summary dialog.
Must memorise · Choose prices that let the floor fire

The question lets you pick the three prices. That freedom is a trap with a right answer.

Pick 15000, 12000 and 9000 and part 3's price floor can never fire. The largest possible discount is 25%, so nothing ever falls near 50.0. You will have written a floor you cannot demonstrate and the examiner cannot see work.

Pick 30.0, 25.0 and 20.0 and the floor becomes live: one Gold day is 30, less 15% is 25.50, which is below 50.0, so the method returns 50.0. The 50.0 floor is itself the hint about the scale the examiner had in mind.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question lets you choose the numbers, choose numbers that make every rule visible. A rule that never fires is a rule you cannot be shown to have written correctly.

Teach · What "nested, not separate" actually means here

Part 2 is unusually explicit: nested if-else, not a switch, not independent if checks, and "the nesting must reflect that days attending is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check."

So the shape is forced. The tier decides the branch; the days are examined inside it:

What the question demandsWhat loses the mark
if (Gold) { if (days == 3) 25 else 15 }
else if (Silver) { if (days == 3) 15 else 5 }
else { 0 }		 if (Gold && days == 3) 25;
if (Gold && days < 3) 15;
if (Silver && days == 3) 15;
Right answers, wrong structure: days is tested at the top level, four separate times. This is what "not independent checks" forbids.

Why the final else is the whole Bronze rule. "Any tier string that is not Gold or Silver must be treated as Bronze" is not an extra check you add: it is what a bare else already means. Write else if (tier.equals("Bronze")) and you have broken the rule, because "Platinum" would then match nothing and fall through with no discount assigned. The bare else catches Bronze, Platinum, "gold" in lower case, and an empty string, which is exactly what was asked (Unit 4.4).

The same else must also do the counting. If "Platinum" is treated as Bronze for the discount, it is a Bronze attendee in the summary too. Count it anywhere else and your dialog contradicts your own pricing.

Code · question five, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ConferenceTickets {    // Part i: a switch returning the base price for a day. Any other day is illegal.    static double basePriceForDay(int day) {        switch (day) {            case 1:  return 30.0;            case 2:  return 25.0;            case 3:  return 20.0;            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(                         "Day must be 1, 2 or 3 but was " + day);        }    }    // Part ii: NESTED if-else. Days are only examined inside a tier branch.    static double discountPercent(String tier, int daysAttending) {        if (tier.equals("Gold")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 25.0;            } else {                return 15.0;            }        } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 15.0;            } else {                return 5.0;            }        } else {            return 0.0;        }    }    // Part iii: apply the discount, with a price floor of 50.0.    static double applyDiscount(double baseTotal, double percent) {        double discounted = baseTotal - (baseTotal * percent / 100.0);        if (discounted < 50.0) {            return 50.0;        }        return discounted;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int attendees = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        double totalRevenue = 0;        int goldCount = 0, silverCount = 0, bronzeCount = 0;        for (int a = 1; a <= attendees; a++) {            int days = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            String tier = in.nextLine();            double baseTotal = 0;            for (int d = 1; d <= days; d++) {                baseTotal += basePriceForDay(d);            }            double percent = discountPercent(tier, days);            double finalPrice = applyDiscount(baseTotal, percent);            totalRevenue += finalPrice;            if (tier.equals("Gold")) {                goldCount++;            } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {                silverCount++;            } else {                bronzeCount++;            }            System.out.println("Attendee " + a + ": " + tier + ", " + days                + " day(s), base "                + baseTotal + ", discount " + percent + "%, pays " + finalPrice);        }        System.out.println("SUMMARY");        System.out.println("Total revenue: " + totalRevenue);        System.out.println("Gold: " + goldCount + ", Silver: " + silverCount            + ", Bronze: " + bronzeCount);    }}
OutputAttendee 1: Gold, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 25.0%, pays 56.25
Attendee 2: Gold, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 15.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 3: Silver, 2 day(s), base 55.0, discount 5.0%, pays 52.25
Attendee 4: Bronze, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 0.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 5: Platinum, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 0.0%, pays 75.0
SUMMARY
Total revenue: 283.5
Gold: 2, Silver: 1, Bronze: 2

Read attendees 2 and 4: both would have paid less than 50 and both paid exactly 50.0, so the floor is visibly working. Read attendee 5: "Platinum" got a 0% discount and was counted as Bronze, so the two Bronze rules agree. Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed; in the hall, every prompt is JOptionPane.showInputDialog and the summary is one showMessageDialog (F.11).

Trap · The switch must return, or fall through

Part 1's method must give back a price for 1, 2 and 3 and throw otherwise. Writing return inside each case is what makes that safe: a return leaves the method immediately, so no break is needed and there is no fall-through to worry about (Unit 4.3).

Use double price; with assignments instead and you must not forget the breaks, and the compiler will additionally complain that price "might not have been initialized" unless every path assigns it. The default: throw is what convinces the compiler every path is covered: an exception is a legitimate way to leave a method that promised to return a double, because it does not return at all.

Note also that throw needs no throws clause here. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked (Unit 10.1), which is Q1 B's distinction being examined a second time on the same paper.
